content:
An online store should send a small set of automated email and WhatsApp messages across each customer's life with the shop: a welcome when they subscribe, a nudge when they browse or abandon a cart, clear order updates, a check-in and review request after delivery, a replenishment or cross-sell reminder, and a win-back note when they go quiet. These "lifecycle flows" are built once, run every day, and for most small stores bring in more repeat orders than occasional festival blasts do. In ecommerce website development in Pune we treat them as part of the store build, not as something the marketing team adds later, because they depend on things the website has to get right: consent capture at signup and checkout, clean order and product data, events passed to the messaging tool, and a sending domain that mailbox providers trust.

This guide is for owners and marketing managers of Indian D2C and retail stores on Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom platform. It explains which flows to build and in what order, what each message should say, how to split work between email and WhatsApp, the consent and sender rules that decide whether messages arrive at all, how to connect it to the store, and how to measure whether it is working.

## Campaigns versus flows

A **campaign** is a one-off message to a list: the Diwali sale, a new collection. A **flow** (also called an automation or journey) is triggered by something an individual customer does or does not do: subscribing, leaving a cart, receiving an order, not buying for 90 days.

Flows matter for three reasons.

- **Timing.** A message about the product a person looked at an hour ago is more relevant than anything you can send to the whole list.
- **They compound.** Every new subscriber and customer passes through them without anyone pressing send.
- **They are gentler on your sender reputation.** Messages people expect get opened and are rarely marked as spam, which helps your campaigns reach the inbox too.

How much revenue flows produce varies by category, price and repeat-purchase cycle. Vendors publish benchmarks that show automated messages earning far more per send than campaigns, but they are drawn from each vendor's own customers; treat them as direction, not a forecast, and measure your own.

## What the website must capture first

No tool can fix missing consent or missing data. Before choosing software, make sure the store does the following.

### Consent, recorded properly

- **Email signup forms** (footer, pop-up, account creation) that say what the person will receive, with the source and timestamp stored.
- **A checkout marketing checkbox** for email, unticked by default, separate from the order itself. Order emails do not need marketing consent; newsletters do.
- **A separate WhatsApp opt-in**, naming your business and WhatsApp explicitly: "Send me order updates and offers on WhatsApp". Meta's WhatsApp Business policy requires that a business obtain opt-in before messaging people, and consent to email is not consent to WhatsApp.
- **Easy opt-out** on both channels, honoured immediately across your systems.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 points the same way: consent should be specific, informed and as easy to withdraw as to give. Its rules were notified in November 2025 and most obligations take effect 18 months later, so building consent records correctly now saves rework. See our guides to [WhatsApp opt-in compliance](/blog/whatsapp-opt-in-compliance-checklist) and [cookie consent under the DPDP Act](/blog/web-development-company-pune-cookie-consent-banner-block-scripts-dpdp-2026).

### Events and data

The messaging tool needs to know what happens on the store. At minimum:

- viewed product, added to cart, started checkout (with the items);
- placed order, order fulfilled, order delivered, order cancelled or refunded;
- customer created, subscribed, unsubscribed;
- product catalogue with titles, images, prices, URLs and stock.

On Shopify and WooCommerce, the main email and WhatsApp tools provide integrations that send most of this. On a custom store, your developer has to send these events through the tool's API, and "delivered" usually has to come from your courier or shipping aggregator's webhook.

### A sending domain mailbox providers trust

Send from your own domain (`hello@yourstore.in`), not a free Gmail address, and authenticate it. Google's sender guidelines require all senders to Gmail to set up SPF or DKIM, and require those who send more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail accounts to set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC, align the From domain, offer one-click unsubscribe on marketing messages and keep spam rates reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.3%, while recommending you stay under 0.1%. Yahoo applies similar rules. A small store will rarely reach 5,000 a day, but the same set-up is good practice at any size. Our article on [email deliverability, SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/web-development-company-pune-email-deliverability-spf-dkim-dmarc-2026) walks through it.

## Email or WhatsApp: which channel for which message

| | Email | WhatsApp |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | Low; priced by contacts or sends on most tools | Meta charges per delivered template message, by category and country; your provider may add its own fee |
| Rules | Consent and unsubscribe; mailbox provider sender rules | Opt-in; pre-approved templates outside the 24-hour customer service window; quality rating and messaging limits |
| Good for | Longer content, several products, receipts, newsletters | Short, timely, personal messages; order updates; replies |
| Risk if overused | Lands in Promotions or spam | Blocks and reports lower your quality rating and can limit your sending |

WhatsApp templates fall into categories: **marketing**, **utility** (updates about an order or account the customer already has) and **authentication** (OTPs). Meta decides the category from the content, and a "utility" template that carries an offer is treated as marketing. Since July 2025 Meta has charged per template message rather than per conversation; rates change, so check Meta's current rate card rather than relying on a blog post. Our explainer on [utility versus marketing templates](/blog/whatsapp-utility-vs-marketing-templates) covers the distinction.

A practical rule for Indian stores: use **WhatsApp for what is urgent and expected** (order confirmation, shipping, delivery, a single cart reminder) and **email for what is rich or frequent** (welcome series, education, product recommendations, newsletters). Use the paid WhatsApp marketing message where its higher attention pays for itself, and do not send the same content on both channels at the same moment.

## The seven flows to build, in order

### 1. Order and shipping updates

These are transactional, expected and the most read messages you will ever send. Get them right before any marketing.

- **Order confirmation**: items, total, delivery address, expected delivery window, how to get help.
- **Shipped**: tracking link.
- **Out for delivery** and **delivered**.
- **Delayed, cancelled or refunded**: plain and prompt.

Send them by email and, where the customer opted in, as WhatsApp utility templates. Keep offers out of them. Our article on the [order confirmation page and transactional emails](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-order-confirmation-page-transactional-emails-2026) covers the content in detail.

### 2. Welcome series

**Trigger:** someone subscribes without having bought.

- **Message 1, immediately:** deliver what you promised (the discount code, the guide), say who you are in two lines, and show your three best-selling products.
- **Message 2, after 2–3 days:** why you exist or how the product is made; real customer photos or reviews.
- **Message 3, after 5–7 days:** help choosing (a size guide, a "which one is for me" comparison), and a reminder if the welcome offer is about to expire.

Stop the series the moment the person buys. If you use a welcome discount, make the code single-use and time-limited so it does not end up on coupon sites.

### 3. Abandoned cart and abandoned checkout

**Trigger:** items added or checkout started, no order within a set time.

- **Message 1, after about 1 hour:** "You left this behind", with the product image and a link straight back to the cart. No discount.
- **Message 2, after about 24 hours:** answer the likely objection: delivery time, returns, cash on delivery availability, a review.
- **Message 3, after 2–3 days (optional):** a small incentive, if your margins allow, and only for people who have not bought before.

Leading with a discount trains customers to abandon carts on purpose. We cover this flow fully in [abandoned cart recovery](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-abandoned-cart-recovery-2026).

### 4. Browse abandonment

**Trigger:** a known subscriber viewed a product two or more times, or a category repeatedly, without adding to cart.

One email, a day later: the product, two similar ones, and help ("Not sure about the size? Reply to this email"). Keep it to email; a WhatsApp message saying "we saw you looking" feels intrusive. Cap it so nobody receives more than one a week.

### 5. Post-purchase

**Trigger:** order delivered. This is the flow most stores skip and the one that most affects repeat purchase.

- **Day 0–1 after delivery:** how to use or care for the product; a short video or guide; how to reach support. This reduces returns and complaints.
- **Day 5–10 (longer for products that take time to judge):** a review request, with a direct link to the review form for the item bought. Ask every customer in the same way, and do not offer a reward only for positive reviews.
- **Day 14–21:** a relevant cross-sell: the matching item, the refill, the accessory. Base it on what was bought, not on what you want to clear.

Start the timers from the delivery event, not from the order date. Asking for a review of a parcel that has not arrived is the commonest mistake in this flow. Our guide to [product reviews and rating systems](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-product-reviews-ratings-system-2026) explains how to collect and display them.

### 6. Replenishment and repeat purchase

**Trigger:** time since the last order of a consumable, based on how long it lasts.

If a 200 g pack of coffee, a face wash or a month's supplements typically lasts 30 days, send a reminder at around day 24 with a one-tap reorder link. Work out the interval from your own order data (the median gap between repeat orders of that product) rather than guessing. For non-consumables, use a "what goes with it" or "new arrivals in the category you bought" message at a sensible interval instead.

### 7. Win-back and sunset

**Trigger:** no order and no engagement for a period that fits your category: perhaps 60–90 days for consumables, 6–12 months for furniture or jewellery.

- **Message 1:** what is new since they last bought, their past favourites.
- **Message 2, a week later:** an incentive, if you use them.
- **Message 3:** "Do you still want to hear from us?" with one button to stay.

Then **stop emailing people who do not respond**. Continuing to send to inactive addresses lowers your open rates and raises spam complaints, which damages delivery to the customers who do want your emails. Suppress them from regular campaigns and keep them only for rare major announcements, or remove them.

### Occasional flows worth adding later

- **Back in stock** and **price drop** alerts for people who asked.
- **Birthday or anniversary** messages, if you collect the date with consent.
- **VIP** recognition after a third or fifth order.

## Frequency, priority and quiet hours

Flows collide. A new subscriber who abandons a cart on day two could receive a welcome email, a cart email, a cart WhatsApp message and Sunday's campaign within 48 hours. Set rules:

- **Priority:** transactional first, then cart, then post-purchase, then welcome, then campaigns. While someone is in a cart or post-purchase flow, pause the welcome series.
- **Caps:** for example, no more than one marketing WhatsApp message a week and three or four marketing emails a week per person. Choose your own numbers and watch unsubscribes and blocks.
- **Quiet hours:** hold marketing messages between about 9 pm and 9 am. Order updates can go at any time.
- **Exclusions:** do not send a cart reminder to someone who has just bought the same item in a different session; do not send offers to someone with an open complaint.

## Building it on your platform

- **Shopify:** email tools such as Klaviyo, Omnisend, Mailchimp and Shopify's own Email and Flow apps integrate directly; WhatsApp is added through a WhatsApp Business solution provider that has a Shopify app. Check that the tool receives checkout-started and fulfilment events, not only orders.
- **WooCommerce:** the same tools connect by plugin. Confirm compatibility with High-Performance Order Storage and the Checkout block, and that the plugin does not slow the checkout page.
- **Custom stores:** your developer sends events to the tool's API and exposes a product feed. Budget time for this; it is where custom builds usually fall short.

Whichever platform you use:

- Keep **one customer record** with both email and phone, so opt-outs and purchase history apply across channels.
- Use **the store's own product data** in messages (image, price, stock) and hide out-of-stock items from recommendations.
- Add **UTM parameters** to every link so that GA4 can attribute sessions and orders to each flow.
- **Test with real orders** before launch: place an order, abandon a cart, mark an order delivered, unsubscribe. Check every message on an Android phone, in Gmail and in the WhatsApp app.

We set up [WhatsApp automation](/whatsapp/automation) and [WhatsApp Flows](/services/whatsapp-flow) alongside the store when we build it.

## Measuring whether it works

For each flow, track:

- **Sent, delivered, opened or read, clicked.** Email open rates are inflated by Apple Mail's privacy feature, so rely more on clicks.
- **Orders and revenue attributed**, with the attribution window written down. Tools default to generous windows (an order within several days of an open). Shorten the window, and count email on clicks rather than opens, for a more honest figure.
- **Unsubscribes, spam complaints and WhatsApp blocks** per message. A message with high revenue and high complaints is borrowing from your future.
- **Revenue per recipient**, which lets you compare flows of different sizes.

Then look at the business measures the flows are meant to move: repeat purchase rate, the share of customers who place a second order within 90 days, and the time between first and second order. Where your tool allows, keep a small holdout group that receives no marketing flows, and compare its repeat rate with everyone else's. That is the only way to see what the flows cause, as opposed to what they claim.

Review quarterly: update the best-sellers in the welcome series, retire expired offers, and check that every link still works.

## A worked example

This is an illustration with made-up numbers, not a client result.

A Pune skincare brand has 6,000 email subscribers, 2,200 customers with WhatsApp opt-in and about 900 orders a month. It sends two campaigns a month and has only a default abandoned-cart email.

In the first month it builds: order updates on both channels; a three-email welcome series; a cart flow with one WhatsApp reminder at one hour and emails at 24 and 72 hours; a post-purchase flow with a usage guide at delivery, a review request at day 10 and a cross-sell at day 20; and a replenishment reminder at day 26 for its 30-day products.

Three months later the owner looks at four numbers: the review count on product pages, the cart recovery rate, the share of first-time customers who reorder within 90 days, and the WhatsApp block rate. If reviews and reorders have risen and blocks are steady, the flows stay. If the block rate has climbed, the WhatsApp cart reminder is the first thing to soften. The point of the example is the method: build a few flows, choose the measures in advance, and adjust.

## What it typically costs

Indicative figures for India in 2026:

- **Email platform:** free tiers exist for small lists; paid plans scale with contacts and commonly run from a few hundred to several thousand rupees a month for small stores. Check current pricing on the vendor's site.
- **WhatsApp:** a provider subscription (often about ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 a month for small businesses, more for larger teams) plus Meta's per-message charges for templates.
- **Set-up:** designing templates, writing copy, building the seven core flows, integrating and testing: roughly ₹25,000 to ₹90,000 one-off, depending on platform and how many messages need custom design. Custom-store integrations cost more.
- **Ongoing:** monthly review and optimisation, typically ₹8,000 to ₹30,000 if outsourced.

## Frequently asked questions

### What email flows should an online store set up first?

Start with order and shipping updates, then a welcome series for new subscribers, an abandoned cart flow, and a post-purchase flow that gives usage help and asks for a review after delivery. Add browse abandonment, replenishment reminders and a win-back flow once those are working.

### Is WhatsApp or email better for ecommerce marketing in India?

Use both for different jobs. WhatsApp is read quickly and suits order updates and a single timely reminder, but each template message is charged and overuse leads to blocks. Email costs little per message and suits longer content, product recommendations and newsletters. Do not send the same message on both at once.

### Do I need customer consent to send WhatsApp marketing messages?

Yes. Meta's WhatsApp Business policy requires a business to obtain opt-in before messaging people, and messages sent outside the 24-hour customer service window must use approved templates. Collect a separate, clearly worded WhatsApp opt-in at signup or checkout and honour opt-outs immediately.

### How many abandoned cart messages should a store send?

Two or three is typical: a reminder after about an hour, a second after about a day that answers likely doubts, and an optional third after two to three days with a small incentive. Stop as soon as the customer orders, and avoid opening with a discount.

### Why are my store's marketing emails going to spam?

Common causes are sending from an unauthenticated or free email address, missing SPF, DKIM or DMARC records, emailing people who never subscribed or have not opened in months, and no easy unsubscribe. Google requires bulk senders to authenticate, offer one-click unsubscribe and keep spam complaint rates below 0.3%.
